========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, what brings me in... I guess I've just completely stopped wanting to do the things that usually keep me going. Like, I haven't even been walking into my shop lately just to enjoy the smell of the wood. And I usually love that smell. I've been a carpenter a long time, and there's nothing quite like the scent of fresh cut cedar or mahogany. I was actually working on a cedar chest for my niece's wedding—she got married up in Portland a few weeks ago. Beautiful outdoor ceremony, though it rained right at the end. You know how the weather is up there, you can't ever trust a clear sky. Her new husband is a nice enough guy, works in IT or something with computers. I don't really understand how a man can spend all day just staring at a screen, to be honest with you. 

But anyway, I just... I don't have the drive for my shop anymore. Or for anything else, really. I've stopped going to my salsa nights, haven't been to the church gatherings at all. I usually cook for the neighbors, too. I always make this big batch of smoked brisket or chili for the block. Mrs. Higgins next door always returns my Tupperware with a little slice of lemon pound cake—she's a sweet lady, lost her husband a few years back. But yeah, I just haven't had it in me to fire up the smoker or see anyone. I just don't care about doing any of it anymore.

Well... yeah, I guess I have. I mean, I've had these thoughts lately where I just think... maybe it would be easier if I just didn't wake up at all. Yeah, the guys at the job site have been on my case about it. They say half the time I'm moving like my boots are full of wet cement, taking forever just to pick up a single board. Which, actually, I really did get my boots stuck in wet cement once. Back in '98, we were doing this big driveway pour for a guy who owned a car dealership. He wanted this fancy stamped concrete, paid a fortune for it. Well, the kid running the screed board tripped and I had to jump right in the mix to catch it before he ruined the grade. Ruined a perfectly good pair of Red Wing boots. You can't just wash that stuff off once it starts to cure, you know, it just eats right through the leather. I tried taking them to a cobbler, this old Italian guy downtown, but he just took one look and laughed at me. His shop smelled amazing, though, like shoe polish and strong espresso. He had this antique brass cash register that must have weighed two hundred pounds. But anyway, yeah, if I'm not moving in slow motion, it's the other way around. I'll just get stuck pacing around the shop, rubbing my hands together over and over, and not actually doing anything useful at all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yeah, I have. I mean, it's just heavy on my chest all the time. I keep replaying every single doctor's appointment, every little change in my wife's health... I just keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner, you know? Like I should have protected her somehow. 

We used to go to this doctor, Dr. Henderson. Nice guy, had these old Norman Rockwell paintings in his waiting room. I always liked the one with the kid at the soda fountain. He built this incredible oak dining table for my grandmother that we still have in our house. Weighs an absolute ton. We tried moving it when we repainted the dining room last spring, and I swear I almost threw my back out. We painted it this color called "Sea Salt," which my wife picked out. She loves those coastal colors. Reminds her of our honeymoon in Cape Cod. We ate so much lobster on that trip I thought I was gonna turn red. 

But yeah, I just... I can't stop thinking that if I'd paid closer attention, maybe she wouldn't be going through all this, and it's my fault I didn't see the signs.

Yeah, well, before this whole cement-boots feeling set in, I had this crazy surge going on. I literally could not sit still. I was up late into the night, just sketching out all these new workshop ideas, calling up suppliers, and hunting for the next thing to fix before I had even finished the first project.

Yeah, pretty much every day. It's like this heavy weight, you know? I just... I keep replaying every single doctor's appointment, every little change in my wife’s health over the last few years. I keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner, or... or protected her somehow.

The traffic out there on Route 9 is always a nightmare because of the farmers' market they set up right off the highway. People just slam on their brakes to turn in for fresh tomatoes. I don't get it, honestly. You can buy perfectly good tomatoes at the Stop & Shop down the street. Although, I will say, the supermarket tomatoes always taste kind of watery compared to the ones my grandfather used to grow. He had this massive garden in his backyard. I hated going down there as a kid because there were these huge wolf spiders that would hang out near the water heater. I’m still terrified of spiders. Last week I saw one in the garage near my workbench, right next to my circular saw. I actually left the garage and didn't go back in for two days. My son had to come over and kill it for me. He laughed at me, of course. Kids always think they're tougher than their old man once they hit their twenties...

But yeah, the worthlessness... it's there every day. Just constantly thinking I failed her when she needed me most.

Mrs. Higgins next door always returns my Tupperware with a little slice of lemon pound cake—she's a sweet lady, lost her husband a few years back. But yeah, I just haven't had it in me to fire up the smoker or see anyone. It was real sudden, and it just completely wrecked our daily routine. We used to have things so set, you know? Like, every morning we’d sit on the back porch with our coffee. The salsa nights, the church gatherings, cooking for the neighbors... it's all just gone flat. \n\nI actually tried to go to church a few weeks ago, thinking it might help. But anyway, yeah... even when I try to do those things now, I just don't get any joy out of them at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or how quickly you're able to perform daily tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, my energy is just shot. My buddy Dave used to run one in his garage with the door shut tight, gave himself mild carbon monoxide poisoning. He's fine now, but they kept him overnight at the hospital for observation. He complained the whole time about the food. Said they just gave him green Jell-O and a piece of dry meatloaf. I never understood why hospitals always push Jell-O on you. Is it supposed to be medicinal or something? My wife makes this cherry Jell-O mold for Thanksgiving with the little mandarin oranges inside, but that's a whole different ballgame. \n\nBut yeah, to answer you, it's just like I mentioned before—I get stuck in that pacing rut, just fidgeting and walking in circles instead of working.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling guilty about anything in particular lately?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I have. I mean, it's just heavy on my chest all the time. I keep replaying every single doctor's appointment, every little change in my wife's health... I just keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner, you know? Like I should have protected her somehow. \n\nWe used to go to this doctor, Dr. Henderson. Nice guy, had these old Norman Rockwell paintings in his waiting room. I always liked the one with the kid at the soda fountain. You don't see soda fountains anymore, do you? When I was a kid, my granddad used to take me to the pharmacy down on Main Street and they had a real marble counter. We'd get these cherry phosphates. Best thing I ever tasted. Granddad was a carpenter, too, actually. Taught me how to hold a hammer when I was just five years old. He built this incredible oak dining table for my grandmother that we still have in our house. Weighs an absolute ton. We tried moving it when we repainted the dining room last spring, and I swear I almost threw my back out. We painted it this color called \"Sea Salt,\" which my wife picked out. She loves those coastal colors. Reminds her of our honeymoon in Cape Cod. We ate so much lobster on that trip I thought I was gonna turn red. \n\nBut yeah, I just... I can't stop thinking that if I'd paid closer attention, maybe she wouldn't be going through all this, and it's my fault I didn't see the signs.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed yourself speaking more slowly than usual over the past two months?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I think I already mentioned that a minute ago, didn't I? The guys at the site are always on my case about it. They say I'm moving like my boots are full of wet cement, like it takes me forever just to pick up a single piece of lumber. \n\nSpeaking of lumber, the price of pine has gone absolutely through the roof lately. I went down to the supplier last week, and I couldn't believe it. I told the guy, \"Are these boards lined with gold?\" He just laughed, but it's no joke when you're trying to bid a job. Used to be you could build a whole deck for what they're charging for a stack of two-by-fours now. My buddy Frank builds these massive wrap-around porches out in the county, and he's had to start using this composite decking material instead. It looks okay, I guess, but it doesn't have the same feel as real wood. Real wood has a soul, you know? You can smell the sap when you cut into it. My grandfather used to say you could tell a lot about a man by how he treated his tools and his timber. He kept his chisels so sharp you could shave with them. He had this old leather strop hanging by his workbench... \n\nBut anyway, yeah, they say I'm talking and moving way slower than normal. I was up late into the night, just sketching out all these new workshop ideas, calling up suppliers, and hunting for the next thing to fix before I had even finished the first project. \n\nSpeaking of sketching, I still use those old-school yellow Dixon Ticonderoga pencils. Number twos. You know the ones? The eraser on those things is actually decent. Most pencils nowadays, the eraser just smudges the graphite everywhere and ruins the paper. I buy them by the gross from this little office supply store downtown. The guy who runs it, Mr. Higgins, he’s been there since the eighties. He’s got this massive collection of vintage typewriters in the back of the shop. Really beautiful machines. Underwood, Royal, Smith Corona. He let me type on this 1930s Underwood once, and the keys take so much force to press down, your fingers actually get a workout. Makes you appreciate modern keyboards, even if they feel cheap and plasticky. My grandson has this mechanical keyboard for his computer games that lights up in all these crazy rainbow colors. Looks like a disco in his bedroom. I don't get the appeal of playing games in the dark like that, honestly. It's gotta be terrible for your eyes. My mom used to yell at me for reading comics by flashlight under the covers when I was a kid... \n\nBut anyway, yeah. I was just running on that surge, jumping from one fix-it job to the next without finishing anything.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that your feelings of guilt are interfering with your daily life most of the time?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I'd say it is. It's just... I can't focus on the work anymore. It's a whole domino effect. I learned that from this old foreman I worked under when I was first starting out, guy named Sal. Sal was a character. Always had an unlit cigar in his mouth, just chewing on it all day long. Said he quit smoking in '85 but missed the feel of it. He drove this beat-up old Ford F-150 that was more rust than metal. The tailgate wouldn't even latch, so he had it held shut with a bungee cord. Haven't been to church in weeks, ignoring my friends, the neighbors... The theater shut down back in the nineties, but they still have the marquee up. They used to show double features on Saturdays for three bucks. I took my wife there on our first date, actually. We saw some terrible sci-fi movie about giant ants or something, I don't even remember the name of it. We shared a large popcorn, and she accidentally spilled half of it on the floor when a rat ran across the aisle. She screamed so loud the projectionist actually stopped the film. We still laugh about that. Popcorn at the movies is a total rip-off now anyway. You go in there and they want ten dollars for a bucket of stale corn and fake butter. I started sneaking in my own snacks in my coat pockets. The kids think it's embarrassing, but I refuse to pay those prices. My daughter, she's in college now, she told me they check your bags at the door at the theater near her campus...\n\nBut yeah, I do feel like a burden. Thinking they'd be better off if I wasn't around, it just... it creeps in, you know?\n\nDoctor: Would you say your feelings of worthlessness are present nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Yeah, pretty much every day. We'd drive out to the county fairgrounds, usually on a Sunday morning. The traffic out there on Route 9 is always a nightmare because of the farmers' market they set up right off the highway. Well, like I was just saying, doc, it's not just the last two weeks. It's been dragging on for about six months now. It's definitely been long enough that it no longer feels like just a bad week or ordinary stress, you know? 

Six months... yeah, that would've been right around the time my crew and I were finishing up the wrap-around deck on the Henderson place. Nice folks, the Hendersons. Mrs. Henderson would always bring us out these big pitchers of iced tea around noon. Not the cheap powdered stuff, either. She brewed it real strong with actual tea bags and put fresh mint in it. Said she grew the mint right there in her kitchen window box. Mint is funny like that, you know, it grows like an absolute weed if you aren't careful. My wife tried planting some in our backyard garden a few years back and it completely took over the whole bed. Choked the life right out of her beefsteak tomatoes. We had to dig up the dirt and start completely over the next spring. I bought this organic compost from a farm stand out in the valley to mix into the soil, and let me tell you, it smelled like absolute death. The dog loved it, though. He got out of the house and rolled right in it while I was grabbing my shovel. Had to give him three baths in the driveway with that oatmeal shampoo just to get the stink out. My back was killing me from leaning over the tub... 

But anyway, yeah, to answer your question, it's been a solid six months of this. Not just the last couple of weeks.

Number twos. You know the ones? The eraser on those things is actually decent. Most pencils nowadays, the eraser just smudges the graphite everywhere and ruins the paper. Haven't been to church in weeks, ignoring my friends, the neighbors... I really do. I've been having these thoughts lately, like... maybe it would just be easier if I went to sleep and didn't wake up. You cut the plastic and it just inflates like a life raft. It's supposed to be great for your back, but honestly, I think I liked our old coil spring mattress better. We had that thing for fifteen years. I bought it at this local furniture store that used to be over on Main Street, right next to the old movie theater. The theater shut down back in the nineties, but they still have the marquee up. They used to show double features on Saturdays for three bucks. I took my wife there on our first date, actually. We saw some terrible sci-fi movie about giant ants or something, I don't even remember the name of it. Well, to be honest with you doc, this whole... this whole specific change in my mood and my behavior, it's really been going on for about two months now. That's right around the time my wife's health suddenly declined and our whole daily routine just went completely out the window. 

It was a massive adjustment. We were suddenly having to drive back and forth to the medical center downtown for her, and let me tell you, the parking garage at that place is an absolute nightmare. I don't know who engineered it, but they designed it with these incredibly tight corners. I drive a full-size pickup, and trying to maneuver around those concrete pillars is like threading a needle in the dark. You know, you can usually get paint transfer like that off with a little rubbing compound and a good microfiber cloth if you catch it early enough. You just gotta use small, tight circular motions. You can't press too hard, though, or you'll burn right through the factory clear coat. A lot of guys make that exact mistake. They go out and buy those cheap orbital buffers from the hardware store and just go to town on their doors, and the next thing you know, they're looking at bare primer. Primer isn't meant to be exposed to the weather like that. It actually absorbs moisture, and then before you know it, you get rust bubbling up from underneath the paint...

We had to rent these massive propane torpedo heaters just to keep the guys from freezing to death. You gotta be real careful with those things, though, if you don't ventilate right. My buddy Dave used to run one in his garage with the door shut tight, gave himself mild carbon monoxide poisoning. He's fine now, but they kept him overnight at the hospital for observation. He complained the whole time about the food. Said they just gave him green Jell-O and a piece of dry meatloaf. I never understood why hospitals always push Jell-O on you. Is it supposed to be medicinal or something? My wife makes this cherry Jell-O mold for Thanksgiving with the little mandarin oranges inside, but that's a whole different ballgame. \n\nBut yeah, to answer you, it's just like I mentioned before—I get stuck in that pacing rut, just fidgeting and walking in circles instead of working.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling guilty about anything in particular lately?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I have. I mean, it's just heavy on my chest all the time. I keep replaying every single doctor's appointment, every little change in my wife's health... I just keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner, you know? Like I should have protected her somehow. \n\nWe used to go to this doctor, Dr. Henderson. Nice guy, had these old Norman Rockwell paintings in his waiting room. I always liked the one with the kid at the soda fountain. You don't see soda fountains anymore, do you? When I was a kid, my granddad used to take me to the pharmacy down on Main Street and they had a real marble counter. We'd get these cherry phosphates. Best thing I ever tasted. Weighs an absolute ton. We tried moving it when we repainted the dining room last spring, and I swear I almost threw my back out. We painted it this color called \"Sea Salt,\" which my wife picked out. She loves those coastal colors. Reminds her of our honeymoon in Cape Cod. Used to be you could build a whole deck for what they're charging for a stack of two-by-fours now. My buddy Frank builds these massive wrap-around porches out in the county, and he's had to start using this composite decking material instead. It looks okay, I guess, but it doesn't have the same feel as real wood. Real wood has a soul, you know? You can smell the sap when you cut into it. My grandfather used to say you could tell a lot about a man by how he treated his tools and his timber. He kept his chisels so sharp you could shave with them. He had this old leather strop hanging by his workbench... \n\nBut anyway, yeah, they say I'm talking and moving way slower than normal. Unless I'm doing the opposite and just pacing around the shop rubbing my hands together, getting absolutely nothing done.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling like you're moving more quickly than usual, or like your thoughts are racing?\n\nPatient: Yeah, well, before this whole cement-boots feeling set in, I had this crazy surge going on. I literally could not sit still. I was up late into the night, just sketching out all these new workshop ideas, calling up suppliers, and hunting for the next thing to fix before I had even finished the first project. \n\nSpeaking of sketching, I still use those old-school yellow Dixon Ticonderoga pencils. Number twos. You know the ones? The eraser on those things is actually decent. Most pencils nowadays, the eraser just smudges the graphite everywhere and ruins the paper. I buy them by the gross from this little office supply store downtown. The guy who runs it, Mr. Higgins, he’s been there since the eighties. Haven't been to church in weeks, ignoring my friends, the neighbors...
